title: Every legal document is offered by an unnamed legal person — no Art. 28 contract, no Art. 13 controller identity, no P.D. 131/2003 provider identification
where: locales/en/legal/terms.md:9; locales/en/legal/privacy.md:26; locales/en/legal/dpa.md:9; locales/en/legal/legal-notice.md:13-20 (and the identical Greek files)
what: The Terms, Privacy Policy, DPA and Legal Notice all name the provider as `[COMPANY LEGAL NAME]` at `[REGISTERED ADDRESS]`, GEMI `[COMPANY REGISTRATION NUMBER / GEMI]`, VAT `[VAT NUMBER]` / `[TAX OFFICE]`, legal representative `[NAME(S)]`, contact `[CONTACT EMAIL]`, DPO `[DPO EMAIL]`. Every rendered page additionally carries a permanent banner reading 'Draft — pending review by qualified legal counsel … not legal advice' (apps/web/app/[locale]/legal/page.tsx:30-32 and [doc]/page.tsx:34-36 render `legal.draftNotice` unconditionally). Separately, apps/site/site.config.json names a DIFFERENT controller — the natural person 'Νικόλαος Πινάτσης', Λάρισα — so libriant.com and app.libriant.com publish two incompatible provider identities.
impact: A GDPR Art. 28(3) processor contract must identify the processor; a privacy notice must identify the controller (Art. 13(1)(a)); Greek P.D. 131/2003 (e-Commerce Directive Art. 5) requires legal name, address, GEMI and VAT on the site. None exist. The clickwrap therefore forms no enforceable contract and no valid Art. 28 agreement, so from the first member record entered, Libriant processes public-library patron data — including children's — with no lawful processor arrangement at all. Every target customer is a public body whose DPO will read /legal/dpa, see the draft banner and the empty party name, and stop the procurement. Both the library and Libriant are exposed to HDPA enforcement under Art. 28 + Art. 83(4)(a).
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/terms.md:9 — 'These Terms of Service ("Terms") are a binding agreement between `[COMPANY LEGAL NAME]`, `[REGISTERED ADDRESS]`, company reg. no. `[COMPANY REGISTRATION NUMBER / GEMI]`'. RAN `grep -o '\[[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9 ,/&.()-]*\]' locales/*/legal/*.md | sort | uniq -c` → 12 uppercase placeholders in privacy.md, 9 in terms.md, 9 in legal-notice.md, 4 in dpa.md, per locale. READ apps/site/site.config.json → "controllerName": "Νικόλαος Πινάτσης".
fix: Register the operating entity, then fill every `[PLACEHOLDER]` in all 14 markdown files (7 slugs x 2 locales), make the site's `identity.controllerName` the same entity, have Greek/EU data-protection counsel review, then delete the `legal.draftNotice` string and the two `<Banner>` blocks and bump LEGAL_VERSION. Do not accept a single signup until this is done.

title: Backups are unencrypted and the off-site copy is never pruned — the DPA's 'encrypted backups' TOM is false and erasure never propagates out of backups
what: backup.sh produces `pg_dumpall`→.sql.gz of the control DB plus every tenant DB, a `tar czf` of the storage volume, and a tar of the Caddy access log. There is no gpg/age/openssl step anywhere — `grep -niE 'gpg|encrypt|age|openssl|crypt' scripts/backup.sh` returns only unrelated matches, and scripts/secrets.ts defines only BACKUP_HEARTBEAT_URL, BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS, BACKUP_ALLOW_LOCAL_ONLY (no passphrase). Local dailies are pruned at BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS (default 14, scripts/ensure-env.sh:113). The off-site push is `rclone copy --quiet "$dest" "$RCLONE_REMOTE/$day"` (line 188) — `copy`, not `sync`, into a per-day path, with no `--delete`, no lifecycle rule and no prune step anywhere in the repo. Off-site dailies therefore accumulate forever.
impact: Plain-text SQL dumps of every Greek library's complete member registry — fullName, dateOfBirth, home address, phone, email, staffNotes, and the full loan/reservation/fine history of each named person including school-library children — sit on a Hetzner Storage Box readable by anyone who obtains the rclone credentials or the storage-box snapshot. Art. 32(1)(a) explicitly names encryption; the DPA promises it contractually, so the statement in the binding Art. 28 agreement is untrue. Because off-site copies are never deleted, an Art. 17 erasure or a tenant hard-delete never reaches the backups — the Privacy Policy's 'deleted copies age out of backups' is false in the deployed design, not merely in a placeholder.
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/dpa.md:88 — '…regular **encrypted** backups with restore testing'. READ locales/en/legal/privacy.md:85 — 'Backups: rotated on a rolling `[14]`-day cycle, after which deleted copies age out of backups.' RAN `grep -niE 'gpg|encrypt|age|openssl|crypt' scripts/backup.sh` → no encryption call. READ scripts/backup.sh:188 `rclone copy --quiet "$dest" "$RCLONE_REMOTE/$day"`; RAN `grep -n 'rclone' scripts/backup.sh` → one call, no delete/prune of the remote.
fix: Encrypt each artefact before it leaves the box (`age -r <recipient>` or `gpg --symmetric` with a key held outside the host, or an `rclone crypt` remote) and record the key-management story in the DPA Annex II. Add a remote-retention step (`rclone delete --min-age ${BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS}d` or a storage-box lifecycle policy) and prove it in scripts/dr-drill.sh. Only then may the DPA say 'encrypted' and the Privacy Policy say copies age out.

title: Erasure does not erase: the only member deletion is a soft archive, and the DPA states the opposite
what: `DELETE /members/:id` routes to `archive()`, whose entire mutation is `data: { archivedAt: new Date(), status: 'archived' }`. Every column survives: fullName, email, phone, dateOfBirth, addressLine1/2, city, postalCode, photoAssetRef, staffNotes, customFields. Loans, Reservations and Fines keep the memberId FK and their own `notes`. `grep -rn 'member\.delete|\.member\.deleteMany|erase|anonymi|pseudonymi' apps/api/src packages` finds no hard-delete and no anonymisation path in the product — the only `member.deleteMany` in the tree is packages/db-tenant/scripts/smoke-test.ts:86. On top of that the tenant audit_log permanently stores `{memberNumber, fullName, status, email, archivedAt}` in beforeJson/afterJson for every member.created / member.updated / member.archived (members.service.ts:71-87, 371-377, 461-465), with no retention job (see privacy-legal-05).
impact: A Greek public library that receives an Art. 17 request from a patron — or a parent acting for a child — cannot honour it through the product. There is no supported way to remove the person's name, date of birth or home address; the librarian's only options are to overwrite fields by hand (leaving the pre-edit values in the audit log's beforeJson anyway) or to ask Libriant for out-of-band SQL. The controller is in breach of Art. 12(3)/17 with no remedy, and the processor has contractually promised a capability it does not ship.
evidence: READ apps/api/src/members/members.service.ts:456-459 — `await tx.member.update({ where: { id }, data: { archivedAt: new Date(), status: 'archived' } })`. READ locales/en/legal/dpa.md:98 — 'The Service gives you tools to access, correct, export, and delete Controller Personal Data directly.' RAN `grep -rn "member\.delete\|\.member\.deleteMany\|erase\|anonymi\|pseudonymi\|gdpr" apps/api/src apps/web/app packages --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx"` → 7 hits, none an erasure implementation.
fix: Add a real `POST /members/:id/erase` that (a) nulls or tombstones every direct identifier on Member, (b) rewrites the memberId references on Loan/Reservation/Fine to an 'erased member' sentinel or strips their free-text notes, (c) redacts the identifier fields out of the tenant audit_log rows targeting that member, and (d) records only the fact and timestamp of erasure. Until it ships, change DPA §7 to say plainly that erasure requests must be sent to Libriant and are executed manually, and state the SLA.

title: Member personal data is copied into the shared control plane and survives tenant deletion — contradicting the 'separate database per library' TOM in both the Privacy Policy and the DPA
what: The member-notifications job reads `member.fullName`, `member.email` and `copy.book.title` out of the tenant DB and enqueues them as `toEmail` + `bodyMarkdown` rows in the CONTROL-plane `email_outbox` table (one row per due-soon, overdue and hold-ready notice, forever, with no purge). support_action_log likewise stores pre/post state of touched member rows (schema.prisma:901-921) in the control plane. Both `email_outbox.tenantId` and `audit_log.tenantId` are declared `onDelete: SetNull`, so the admin hard-delete path (apps/api/src/admin/admin-tenants.controller.ts:157-217), which drops the tenant database and cascades the control rows, leaves these rows behind with `tenantId = NULL`.
impact: The single security measure both the Privacy Policy and the Art. 28 DPA lead with — 'isolation of each library's data in a separate database' — is untrue for the highest-sensitivity item in the system: an identified person's reading record. Borrowing history can reveal health, religion, politics and sexuality, and for school libraries the data subjects are children. After a library exercises its deletion right under DPA §8, its members' names, e-mail addresses and book titles remain in Libriant's own database, now orphaned: nothing links them to a tenant, so no future erasure or retention sweep can even find them. Under Art. 28(10) a processor that keeps and determines the fate of personal data outside the controller's instructions becomes a controller for that processing, with its own Art. 5/6/13 obligations that nothing here discharges.
evidence: RAN against the live control DB: inserted a tenant `gdprprobe` plus one `email_outbox` row (`toEmail=maria.papadopoulou@example.gr`, body 'Hi Maria Papadopoulou, "Το Κιβώτιο" was due on 2026-08-01…') and one `audit_log` row (beforeJson `{"fullName":"Maria Papadopoulou","email":"maria.papadopoulou@example.gr"}`), then `DELETE FROM tenants WHERE id='gdprprobe';`. Both rows survived with `tenantId` NULL — the SELECT after the delete returned the e-mail address, the member's name and the book title verbatim. RAN the FK query on information_schema: `email_outbox.tenantId → SET NULL`, `audit_log.tenantId → SET NULL`, every other tenant FK CASCADE.
fix: Either stop persisting rendered member-facing bodies (render at send time from ids and store only kind + recipient hash + status), or change `email_outbox.tenantId` and `audit_log.tenantId` to `onDelete: Cascade` and add a short-TTL purge of delivered bodies (privacy-legal-05). Correct Privacy §5 and DPA Annex II so the isolation claim names the exceptions.

title: No retention period is enforced anywhere in the system, while the Privacy Policy states retention periods as placeholders
what: SCHEDULED_JOBS contains nine jobs; not one deletes personal data on age. Nothing purges: control `email_outbox` (member names, e-mails, book titles, reset links), control `audit_log`, tenant `audit_log`, `support_action_log`, `support_redemption_attempts` (IP addresses), `applications` (site-form applicants), or `users.legalAcceptedIp`. `audit_log_retention_days` is declared as a plan feature and seeded per plan (7 / 90 / 365 / 1095 / 3650 / 1_000_000_000 days in packages/db-control/prisma/seed-data.ts), and the tenant schema comment at :562 says retention 'is enforced by a background job' — `grep -rn 'audit_log_retention_days|auditLogRetention|retention' apps/api/src packages` shows the key is never read by any code. Meanwhile Privacy §6 states the retention schedule as `[30]` days post-termination, `[14]`-day backups, `[up to 5–10]` years tax, and security logs `[a limited period, e.g. 90 days]`.
impact: Art. 5(1)(e) storage limitation is not implemented at any layer, and Art. 13(2)(a) requires the retention period (or the criteria) to be stated — four placeholders are not a retention schedule. Concretely: a member archived in 2026 still has their name and e-mail in the tenant audit_log and in email_outbox in 2036; every IP address ever recorded at signup or in an audit event is kept indefinitely; and the plan feature the pricing page implicitly sells ('audit log retention: 90 days on Starter') is not delivered, which is also a consumer-facing misstatement. A library's own DPO cannot document a retention policy for a system that has none.
evidence: READ apps/api/src/jobs/registry.ts:23-83 — the nine registered jobs are support-session-expiry, reservation-pickup-expiry, stripe-webhook-retry, fine-accrual, export-file-cleanup, announcement-publish, book-metadata-refresh, member-notifications, storage-temp-cleanup. RAN `grep -rn "audit_log_retention_days|auditLogRetention|retention" apps/api/src packages --include="*.ts"` → hits only in packages/shared/src/features.ts:113-116 and packages/db-control/prisma/seed-data.ts (six seed values); no reader. RAN `grep -rn "email_outbox|emailOutbox" apps packages scripts infra | grep -i 'delete|purge|prune|clean'` → no matches.
fix: Add a `retention-sweep` job to SCHEDULED_JOBS that (a) deletes tenant audit_log rows older than the tenant's effective `audit_log_retention_days`, (b) nulls `bodyMarkdown`/`toEmail` on email_outbox rows older than N days (30 is ample for delivery troubleshooting) and deletes the rows after 90, (c) deletes support_redemption_attempts and control audit_log rows past a fixed window, (d) deletes `applications` at 12 months to match the published site notice. Then replace the four placeholders in Privacy §6 with the numbers the job actually enforces.

title: Password-reset and e-mail-verification links are stored in cleartext forever in email_outbox, are not covered by the control-export redaction, and land in the Caddy access log that goes into the unencrypted backups
what: The reset body embeds the raw token — `${env.publicAppUrl}/${locale}/login/reset?token=${token}&slug=${slug}` — and the whole body is persisted as `email_outbox.bodyMarkdown`, a column nothing ever clears. The control-plane export redactor protects `users.passwordHash`, `users.inviteToken`, `support_keys.codeHash`, `tenant_db_credentials.*` and `stripe_webhook_events.payloadJson`, and its catch-all `if (/token|secret|passwordhash|password_hash/.test(c))` matches COLUMN NAMES only — `bodymarkdown` matches nothing, so an owner-admin export with scope `control` or `all` ships every reset link, verification link and support-key notification in plaintext to a 24-hour download file. The same URLs traverse Caddy, whose site-wide `log { format json }` block records the request URI including the query string; backup.sh step 3 tars that log into the daily backup, which is unencrypted and pushed off-site forever (privacy-legal-02).
impact: The Redis token TTL (60 minutes) is the only thing limiting exploitation, so a fresh backup, a fresh access log or a fresh control export is an account-takeover kit for any library owner whose reset is in flight. Independently of token validity, `email_outbox` is a permanent, unredacted archive of every transactional message Libriant has ever composed — member names, member e-mail addresses, borrowed book titles, applicant contact details — reachable through an ordinary admin export and through every backup. The `support_keys.codeHash` redaction is defeated in the same stroke, because the support-key notification body carries the code in the clear next to it.
evidence: READ apps/api/src/auth/password-reset.service.ts:79 (`const resetLink = ...?token=${token}...`) and :101 (`bodyMarkdown: body`). READ apps/api/src/export/export-processors.ts:59-72 — SENSITIVE_COLUMNS has no `email_outbox` entry; `isSensitive` tests `column`, not the value. READ infra/caddy/Caddyfile:25-31 — global `log { output file /var/log/caddy/access.log … format json }`, no URI/query filter. READ scripts/backup.sh:169 — `tar -C "$CADDY_LOG_DIR" -czf "$dest/caddy-logs.tar.gz" .`
fix: Stop persisting secret-bearing bodies: store a template id + variables and render at send time, or null `bodyMarkdown` immediately on `delivered`. Add `email_outbox: new Set(['bodymarkdown','toemail','subject'])` to SENSITIVE_COLUMNS regardless. Deliver reset/verification tokens as a POST-ed form value or a fragment (`#token=`) so they never enter a URL path, or add a Caddy log `filter` that scrubs `?token=`.

title: A platform owner-admin can export any library's entire database with no support key, no notice to the library and no audit entry
what: `POST /admin/exports` with `{scope:'tenant', tenantId}` (or `scope:'all'`) is gated only by `AdminAuthGuard` + `@AdminRoles('owner')`. `createForAdmin` inserts an `export_jobs` row and enqueues the job; it writes no `controlDb.auditEvent`, writes nothing to the target tenant's own audit_log, and sends no notification. This sits beside a carefully built consent model for the OTHER access path: support impersonation requires the TENANT to generate a `SupportKey` (schema.prisma:845-876), which is bcrypt-hashed, single-use, expiring, and every action is written to `support_action_log`. The export path bypasses all of it and yields strictly more data — the full members, loans, reservations and fines tables in one file.
impact: Under DPA §3.1 Libriant may process Controller Personal Data only on the library's documented instructions; taking a complete copy of a library's member registry on a Libriant employee's own initiative is not an instruction, and Art. 28(3)(a)/28(10) make that the processor's liability. The library has no way to detect it: the export leaves no trace in the only log the library can see. DPA §9 promises 'the information necessary to demonstrate compliance with Article 28' — for this operation there is none to give.
evidence: READ apps/api/src/export/admin-export.controller.ts:31-34 (`@UseGuards(AdminAuthGuard, AdminRolesGuard)`) and :52-53 (`@Post() @AdminRoles('owner')`). READ apps/api/src/export/export.service.ts:77-106 — the method body creates the exportJob row and enqueues; RAN `grep -rn 'audit' apps/api/src/export/*.ts` → no matches outside specs, and the only global interceptor is SupportAuditInterceptor (apps/api/src/app.module.ts:82-83), which keys on an active support session.
fix: Write a control-plane AuditEvent (`tenant.exported`, actorType admin) AND a tenant-side audit row for every scope='tenant'/'all' export, e-mail the library's owner when their tenant is exported, and require an active tenant-issued SupportKey session for scope='tenant'. Then describe the residual capability in DPA Annex I.

title: The Art. 30(2) record of processing activities does not exist
what: Art. 30(2) obliges every processor to maintain a written record of all categories of processing carried out on behalf of each controller — controller identities, categories of processing, third-country transfers, and a general description of the Art. 32 measures. Nothing of the kind exists in the repository. `grep -rniE 'dpia|record of processing|article 30|ropa|data protection impact' docs locales apps` returns only the two DPA sentences that PROMISE Art. 35 assistance, plus unrelated hits. The Art. 30(5) small-organisation exemption does not apply here on any of its three limbs: the processing is not occasional, it is large-scale relative to the entity, and it includes data of children.
impact: The record is the first document the Hellenic DPA asks for in any inspection or breach follow-up, and a public-body customer's DPO will request it during onboarding due diligence — public authorities are required to document their processors. Not having one is an independent Art. 83(4)(a) infringement and, practically, an immediate procurement blocker for exactly the δημοτικές and school libraries the launch campaign targets.
evidence: RAN `grep -rniE "dpia|record of processing|article 30|art\. 30|ropa|data protection impact" docs locales apps --include="*.md" --include="*.ts"` → hits are docs/brand/name-clearance (EUIPO), the 2026-06 audit findings, and locales/{el,en}/legal/dpa.md:59/67 ('assist … with your obligations under Articles 32–36 … DPIAs'). No Art. 30 record, no DPIA material, in any language.
fix: Write `docs/legal/ropa.md` covering, per controller category: categories of data subjects (members incl. minors, staff/volunteers), categories of data (identity, contact, dateOfBirth, address, photo, borrowing/reservation/fine history, custom fields, staffNotes), purposes, sub-processors and their locations, transfer safeguards, retention, and a summary of the Art. 32 measures that are actually implemented. Keep it versioned with the code and publish it on request.

title: Acceptance is recorded but not evidenced: one global version string, written once, never read, with no archived copy of the accepted text and no re-acceptance flow
what: `LEGAL_VERSION = '2026-06-22'` is a single string covering all seven documents; editing any one of them without bumping it silently invalidates every stored acceptance. Signup writes `legalAcceptedVersion` / `legalAcceptedAt` on Tenant and User and `legalAcceptedIp` on User — and `grep -rn 'legalAccepted' apps/api/src apps/web` shows those are the ONLY five occurrences in the codebase: nothing ever reads them. There is no re-acceptance prompt (the README calls it 'a future flow'), no admin screen showing who accepted what, and no version archive: apps/web/lib/legal.ts loads `locales/<locale>/legal/<slug>.md` from disk, so /legal/terms always renders whatever is at HEAD. Only the owner ever accepts; staff invited later are never asked and their `legalAcceptedVersion` stays NULL.
impact: Art. 5(2) and Art. 7(1) require the controller to be able to DEMONSTRATE what a person agreed to. Here the record is a bare date string pointing at a mutable file. The five launch libraries will accept documents that are, by their own banner, drafts about to be rewritten by counsel — and once rewritten, nothing prompts them to re-accept and nothing preserves what they saw. In a dispute, or in an HDPA file, Libriant cannot produce the accepted text. Combined with privacy-legal-01, the acceptance evidences agreement to an unnamed party's draft.
evidence: READ packages/shared/src/legal.ts:18 `export const LEGAL_VERSION = '2026-06-22';` and :33 `export const SIGNUP_CONSENT_DOCS: readonly LegalDocSlug[] = ['terms', 'privacy'];`. RAN `grep -rn "legalAccepted" apps/api/src apps/web --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx"` → five hits, all in signup.service.ts:148-174; no reader. READ locales/legal-README.md — 'A future "please re-accept the updated terms" flow can compare a user's stored version against LEGAL_VERSION.'
fix: Snapshot the accepted text: store a content hash per document at acceptance (or commit the rendered documents to an immutable, version-addressed path and record the path). Give each document its own version. Add the gate that compares `user.legalAcceptedVersion` to `LEGAL_VERSION` on login and blocks until re-accepted, and an admin view of the acceptance record. Have the launch libraries re-accept the counsel-reviewed version explicitly.

title: The whole contract with a public body rests on one checkbox self-certifying authority, and the liability cap is EUR 0 for every launch customer
what: Signup requires `acceptLegal === true` and nothing else; Terms §2.1 relies on 'If you are accepting on behalf of an organisation, you confirm you are authorised to bind it'. The customers are Greek public and municipal libraries and school libraries — public bodies whose capacity to contract and to appoint a processor is statutory, exercised by a named representative, not by whichever librarian fills in the form. Separately, Terms §10.3 caps aggregate liability at 'the fees you paid or owed in the 12 months before the event … (or `[EUR amount]` where no fees were paid)'. The launch offer is twelve months free for the first five libraries, so for every launch customer the first limb evaluates to zero and the fallback is an unfilled placeholder.
impact: If the librarian could not bind the municipality, there is no Art. 28 contract and no Terms — Libriant is processing a public authority's patron registry with no legal instrument, and the authority is in breach of Art. 28(1) for using a processor it never appointed. On the liability side, the library is asked to hand over a children-inclusive member registry to a counterparty whose stated maximum liability during the entire free period is nothing at all (and a GDPR Art. 82 claim is not capped by a private contract in any case, which the clause does not carve out beyond §10.1). Any competent public-sector legal review rejects both points.
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/terms.md:129-132 — 'each party's total aggregate liability … is capped at the **fees you paid or owed in the 12 months** before the event giving rise to the claim (or `[EUR amount]` where no fees were paid).' READ apps/api/src/auth/dto/signup.dto.ts:115-118 — the only gate is `@Equals(true) acceptLegal`. Cross-referenced with the launch campaign's twelve-months-free offer for the first five libraries.
fix: For public-body customers use a counter-signed order form / DPA (a PDF signed by the library's legal representative) rather than clickwrap, and record the signed instrument against the tenant. Fill `[EUR amount]` with a real figure proportionate to the risk (not zero) and add an express carve-out that the cap does not limit liability under GDPR Art. 82.

title: Support impersonation — Libriant staff acting inside a library's member data — is disclosed nowhere in the DPA or Privacy Policy
what: The product implements a tenant-consented impersonation flow: a tenant user generates a SupportKey, a platform admin redeems it, and for the session's lifetime that admin acts as a tenant user with full access to members, loans and fines, with every request written to `support_action_log` including `beforeJson`/`afterJson` snapshots of the touched records. The mechanism is well built. It is also invisible in the legal layer: `grep -ni 'support|impersonat' locales/en/legal/{dpa,terms,privacy}.md` finds only a Privacy row for 'Support communications', Terms §6 'Support is provided [via email…]' and a passing 'provide and support the Service'. DPA Annex I (§2) does not list it among the nature/purpose of processing, Annex II (§6) does not mention it as a control, and Privacy §10 'Sharing your data' does not mention it.
impact: The controller cannot describe in its own member-facing privacy notice a category of access that actually exists, and cannot assess it in a DPIA. Because the DPA defines the documented instructions as 'these Terms, this DPA, your configuration, and your use of the Service's features' (§3.1), a support session is only weakly inside instructions — the tenant-issued key is the saving grace, but nothing in writing says what a Libriant admin may do with the access or for how long. It also causes member record snapshots to be copied into the control plane (see privacy-legal-04) with no disclosure and no retention.
evidence: RAN `grep -ni "support|impersonat|access your data|our staff" locales/en/legal/dpa.md locales/en/legal/terms.md locales/en/legal/privacy.md` → 5 hits, none describing impersonation. READ packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:901-921 (`SupportActionLog … beforeJson Json? // Pre-mutation state captured by Prisma middleware`).
fix: Add a DPA section describing support access: that it requires a key the library itself issues, its maximum duration, what is logged, where the log lives (control plane), and its retention. Mirror it in Privacy §10 and give libraries wording they can paste into their own member notice.

title: School libraries are a first-class segment and children's data gets no special treatment anywhere in the product, while the DPA promises Art. 35 assistance that does not exist
what: `school` is one of the selectable library types at signup, and `Member.dateOfBirth` is a stored column. Nothing in the codebase branches on it: `grep -rniE 'minor|child|guardian|parent|under 1[368]|dateOfBirth' apps/api/src apps/web/app packages/shared/src` returns no age logic, no guardian contact field, no consent flag, no restriction on automated e-mail to a minor's address, no reduced-retention rule. The DPA acknowledges the exposure squarely — Annex I lists 'your members/patrons (which may include children)' — and then assigns 100% of it to the controller (§3.2), while §4(e) promises assistance 'with your obligations under Articles 32–36 (… DPIAs …)'. No DPIA template, no children-specific guidance and no Art. 35 material exists in the repo (see privacy-legal-08).
impact: A school library processing pupils' borrowing records is squarely inside the HDPA's high-risk criteria (data of vulnerable subjects, systematic processing) and will need a DPIA before go-live. Libriant supplies nothing, so the promise in the signed DPA is unmet from day one. Operationally, a child member's e-mail address receives automated 'you have Το Κιβώτιο overdue' messages with no way for the library to route notices to a guardian instead, and that disclosure is then retained forever in Libriant's control plane (privacy-legal-04). Nothing prevents a librarian entering a pupil's full home address and photo either, with no shortened retention.
evidence: READ packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:42-45 — `enum LibraryType { … school }`. RAN `grep -rniE "minor|child|guardian|parent|under 1[368]|dateOfBirth" apps/api/src apps/web/app packages/shared/src --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx"` → 30 hits, all false positives (damaged/manage/image/pages); zero minor-handling code. READ locales/en/legal/dpa.md:47-48 — 'Categories of data subjects: your members/patrons (which may include children)'.
fix: Ship a DPIA template and a children's-data guidance note for school libraries as part of the legal layer (that is the Art. 28(3)(f) assistance already promised). In the product, add an optional guardian e-mail on Member that automated notifications prefer when `dateOfBirth` indicates a minor, and let a library set a shorter retention for minor records.

title: The DPA is never presented at signup and is not separately accepted
what: `SIGNUP_CONSENT_DOCS = ['terms','privacy']`, and the checkbox renders as 'Έχω διαβάσει και αποδέχομαι τους [Όρους Χρήσης] και την [Πολιτική Απορρήτου]' — two links, neither to /legal/dpa. The only hook is Terms §5: the DPA 'forms part of these Terms'. So the Art. 28 agreement is incorporated by reference into a clickwrap, is never shown, is never separately evidenced, and — like everything else — carries the draft banner and an unnamed processor when the library does go and read it.
impact: Art. 28(9) accepts electronic form, and incorporation by reference is defensible in principle, but the combination here is not: a public-body controller must be able to show it concluded an Art. 28 contract, and the record on file says only that someone ticked a box labelled 'Terms and Privacy Policy'. A DPO reviewing the onboarding will ask for the signed DPA and there will be nothing to send.
evidence: READ packages/shared/src/legal.ts:33. READ locales/el/legal.json — `"consent.pre": "Έχω διαβάσει και αποδέχομαι τους"`, `"consent.and": "και την"`, with the two links rendered at SignupForm.tsx:372-380. READ locales/en/legal/terms.md:50-51 — '…governed by our [Data Processing Agreement](/legal/dpa), which forms part of these Terms.'
fix: Add 'dpa' to SIGNUP_CONSENT_DOCS, name it in the consent label, and record acceptance of each of the three documents with its own version. For public bodies, back it with the counter-signed instrument from privacy-legal-10.

title: The site's published retention and deletion promises for applicants are not implemented, and the notification e-mail keeps a second permanent copy
what: The public privacy notice at libriant.com promises 'If we do not go ahead together: we delete your details at the latest 12 months after we have been in touch, or immediately if you ask us to' and 'you can ask for deletion with a single email … we will answer within 30 days'. The `applications` table (libraryName, city, contactName, contactEmail, phone, currentSystem, message, consent, privacyVersion) has no purge job — SCHEDULED_JOBS contains none. Worse, applications.service.ts enqueues an admin-notification e-mail whose `bodyMarkdown` restates the applicant's details into `email_outbox`, which is also never purged, so deleting the Application row on request still leaves the applicant's name, e-mail and phone in the control plane indefinitely.
impact: A published, dated, version-pinned retention promise that the system cannot keep. The rest of that notice is genuinely careful — the IP is only ever a peppered hash with a one-hour Redis TTL, and the Application model's comment explains why no IP, country or user-agent is stored — which makes the unenforced 12-month rule the one falsifiable claim on the page. An applicant who invokes the promise gets a partial deletion at best.
evidence: READ apps/site/content/privacy.en.md §5. READ packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:1028-1061 (no deletedAt, no TTL). RAN `grep -rn 'application' apps/api/src/jobs/*.ts` → no matches. READ apps/api/src/applications/applications.service.ts:180 (`bodyMarkdown: body`) against the absence of any email_outbox purge.
fix: Add applications and email_outbox to the retention sweep from privacy-legal-05 (12 months for applications; null the body on delivered outbox rows within 30 days), and make the deletion-on-request path delete both the Application row and its outbox rows.

title: No per-data-subject access or portability tooling — the only export is a full-tenant dump restricted to owner/admin
what: The library-facing export takes a format and nothing else: scope is implicitly the whole tenant. There is no 'export this member's data' action anywhere in the API or the web app. To answer one member's Art. 15 or Art. 20 request, a librarian must either produce a dump containing every other member's name, date of birth, address, phone and complete borrowing history — and then hand-extract one person's rows from it — or transcribe the member page by hand and separately reconstruct the loan, reservation and fine history.
impact: The DPA tells the controller the Service provides tools to 'access … and export Controller Personal Data directly'. For a per-subject request it does not, and the workaround (a whole-database export) is itself a fresh risk: an unencrypted file containing the entire registry, sitting downloadable for 24 hours, created every time a member asks a question. Art. 5(1)(c) data minimisation cuts against making that the standard response.
evidence: READ apps/api/src/export/export.dto.ts:8-12 — `class CreateTenantExportDto { format!: ExportFormat }`, no scope or subject. READ apps/api/src/export/tenant-export.controller.ts:33-34 — `@UseGuards(TenantGuard, RolesGuard) @Roles('owner','admin')`. READ locales/en/legal/dpa.md:98.
fix: Add `GET /members/:id/data-export` returning that member's record plus their loans, reservations, fines and the audit rows targeting them, in a machine-readable format — this is a small query and it is the Art. 15/20 answer. Pair it with the erasure endpoint from privacy-legal-03.

title: Cookie Policy is incomplete and its offline-cache claim is contradicted by the code
where: locales/en/legal/cookies.md (Cookies we set table; Local storage section); apps/web/lib/offline.ts:31-43; apps/web/lib/offline-queue.ts:17-33,49
what: Two defects. (a) The table lists only `libriant_session`, `libriant_admin` and `libriant_imp`. The service is fronted by Cloudflare (the site's own notice at apps/site/content/privacy.en.md §4 discloses `__cf_bm`, a 30-minute bot-management cookie); the app's Cookie Policy omits it. (b) The Local storage section says 'cached data is cleared on sign-out and on session loss'. On sign-out that is true (`clearOfflineCaches` calls `clearQueue`). On session loss it is deliberately false: `clearOfflineReadCaches` clears only the page/data caches and leaves the circulation queue intact, by design, and a queued entry carries `label` — a human-readable member name and book title ('Dune → Ada Lovelace') — for up to MAX_QUEUE_AGE_MS = 18 hours.
impact: The strictly-necessary-only position that justifies not showing a consent banner is correct on the evidence (no analytics, no third-party fonts, no external scripts — CSP is `default-src 'self'; script-src 'none'; font-src 'self'` and grep finds no Sentry/GA/Plausible/Google Fonts anywhere), so this is not a banner problem. It is an accuracy problem in a published policy, and the second half understates how long member names persist on a shared circulation desk workstation after a librarian's session expires.
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/cookies.md ('cached data is cleared on sign-out and on session loss'). READ apps/web/lib/offline.ts:31-43 — the A10-02 comment states the queue is left intact on a 401 on purpose. READ apps/web/lib/offline-queue.ts:29 (`label` — 'Human-readable summary for toasts ("Dune → Ada Lovelace")') and :49 (`MAX_QUEUE_AGE_MS = 18 * 60 * 60 * 1000`). RAN `grep -rniE 'sentry|datadog|posthog|plausible|google-analytics|gtag|hotjar' apps packages infra` → no output; RAN `grep -rn 'fonts.googleapis|next/font/google' apps/web packages/ui` → no output.
fix: Add a `__cf_bm` row to the table (strictly necessary, Cloudflare, 30 min) and reword the local-storage paragraph: caches are cleared on sign-out and on session loss; pending offline circulation actions are kept for up to 18 hours so they can be completed, and are cleared on sign-out.

title: The Legal Notice directs users to the EU ODR platform, which was shut down on 20 July 2025
what: The consumer-dispute section links to ec.europa.eu/consumers/odr. The ODR Regulation (EU) 524/2013 was repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/3228 and the platform ceased operating on 20 July 2025; the obligation to link to it went with it. The paragraph then hedges 'The Service is provided to organisations (B2B); consumer-ADR rules may not apply', which is the right position given Terms §2.1.
impact: A dead link presented as a statutory redress route. Small on its own, but it is the kind of detail a public-body reviewer notices and reads as 'this document was not maintained' — which, given the draft banner and the placeholders, reinforces the wrong impression at the worst moment.
evidence: READ locales/en/legal/legal-notice.md:36-38 — 'the EU Online Dispute Resolution platform is available at [ec.europa.eu/consumers/odr]'.
fix: Delete the ODR paragraph (or replace it with a plain statement that the Service is B2B and that disputes go to the courts named in Terms §12) when counsel reviews the document.

title: With EMAIL_DRIVER=console in production, undelivered member notices are marked 'delivered' and their PII accumulates, while the recipient address is still logged
what: The console driver correctly withholds the body outside development — the A12-02 comment and the `isDev` branch are right, so reset tokens do not reach docker logs in production. It still logs the recipient address (`… NOT delivering "${input.subject}" to ${input.to}`), which for member notifications is a patron's e-mail address plus a subject line naming their overdue book. It also returns a synthetic providerId, so the worker writes `status: 'delivered', deliveredAt: new Date()` for a message nobody received. `createEmailDriver` falls through to console for any unrecognised value, with no production guard.
impact: Patron e-mail addresses and the titles they have out land in container logs (journald/docker, shipped and retained by whatever collects them) with no retention rule, in an environment where by definition no e-mail is being sent. And the outbox fills with member names, addresses and book titles marked delivered — data retained for a purpose that was never served, which is precisely what Art. 5(1)(b)/(e) forbid. Any future audit of 'did the member get the notice' reads a false answer.
evidence: READ apps/api/src/email/drivers/console-driver.ts:32-35 — the non-dev branch logs subject and `to`. READ apps/api/src/email/email-worker.ts:195-202 — unconditional `status: 'delivered'` after `driver.send` returns. READ create-email-driver.ts:19-21 — `default: return new ConsoleEmailDriver()`.
fix: Log only the outbox row id in the non-dev branch, not the recipient. Have the console driver mark the row `status: 'dead'` (or a new `not_sent`) outside development instead of `delivered`, and refuse to boot with EMAIL_DRIVER=console when NODE_ENV=production unless an explicit acknowledgement env var is set — the same pattern backup.sh already uses for BACKUP_ALLOW_LOCAL_ONLY.

title: Member-facing e-mails carry a third-party brand footer and no privacy-notice link or controller identification
what:
Every outgoing message has `'

---

Powered by **CyberSystema** — https://cybersystema.com'` appended. For due-soon, overdue and hold-ready notices the recipient is a library patron who has no relationship with CyberSystema, has never been told a third party processes their address, and gets no link to the library's or Libriant's privacy information in the message.
impact: The Art. 13/14 duty is the library's, but the product makes it harder to discharge: the only entity named in the message the member actually receives is one that appears in none of the library's own paperwork. For a school library e-mailing a pupil, an unexplained commercial brand on a message about their borrowed book is exactly the kind of detail that generates a complaint.
evidence:
READ apps/api/src/email/email-worker.ts:24 (`const BRAND_EMAIL_FOOTER = '

---

Powered by **CyberSystema** — https://cybersystema.com'`) and :190 (`bodyMarkdown: row.bodyMarkdown + BRAND_EMAIL_FOOTER`), applied to every kind including `member_due_soon`, `member_overdue`, `member_hold_ready`.
fix: Use a member-facing footer for the three `member_*` kinds that names the sending library, states that e-mail is sent on its behalf by Libriant, and links to the library's privacy page; keep the CyberSystema footer for messages to library staff and admins.

title: What is right, and should not be broken while fixing the rest
what: Recorded so the remediation does not regress it. (a) The Application model's comment is a model of data minimisation and the implementation matches: no IP, no country, no user-agent stored; abuse throttling uses a peppered SHA-256 in Redis with a 3600s TTL, and consent + the privacy-notice version on screen are both persisted as evidence. (b) The marketing site really does make zero third-party requests — `grep -hoE 'https?://[a-z.]+' apps/site/dist/**/*.html` yields only libriant.com and dpa.gr — so its 'no banner because there is nothing to consent to' claim is true and verifiable, exactly as the notice invites the reader to check. (c) The app has no analytics, no Google Fonts and a tight CSP (`default-src 'self'; script-src 'none'; font-src 'self'`). (d) Admin MFA really is mandatory outside development (`adminMfaRequired: bool('ADMIN_MFA_REQUIRED', !isDev)`, enforced at admin-auth.guard.ts:65), so that Annex II claim holds. (e) Support access is genuinely tenant-consented via a bcrypt-hashed, single-use, expiring key. (f) The password-reset token is claimed atomically with GETDEL and invalidates existing sessions.
impact: None — this is the baseline the eight blockers and highs sit on top of. It is worth stating because several fixes above (retention sweeps, export redaction, member erasure) touch these paths.
evidence: RAN `grep -rhoE 'https?://[a-zA-Z0-9.-]+' apps/site/dist/*.html apps/site/dist/**/*.html | sort -u` → `https://libriant.com`, `https://www.dpa.gr`. RAN `grep -rniE 'sentry|datadog|posthog|plausible|google-analytics|gtag|hotjar' apps packages infra` → no output. READ apps/api/src/config/env.ts:311 and apps/api/src/admin/admin-auth.guard.ts:65. READ packages/db-control/prisma/schema.prisma:1005-1027.
fix: No change required. Preserve these properties when implementing privacy-legal-03, -05 and -06.
